Summary  
Data source overview: The paper analyses how intrinsic properties of autonomous AI systems (opacity, unpredictability, self-learning) make it hard for victims to prove causation after accidents. Through three case studies—cleaning robots, delivery drones and educational robots—it argues existing fault-based liability regimes leave many harms uncompensated and recommends revising liability rules to shift or remove the burden of proof from victims.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[83] – The fabric follows the prescribed node categories, all nodes are connected, no risk→intervention shortcuts, and the JSON validates.  

Inference strategy justification: Where the text only implied concrete legal actions (e.g. “need to revise liability regimes”), I converted them into explicit interventions (“Legislate strict liability…”, “Legislate burden-of-proof reversal…”) marked as Lifecycle 5, Maturity 1 and with confidence 2 to flag light inference. No further speculative steps were introduced.  

Extraction completeness explanation: All reasoning elements explicitly discussed (risk, causation problems, inadequacy of traditional liability, need to shift burden, proposed strict liability / presumption mechanisms, empirical support via case studies) are captured. The three separate legal mechanisms and their downstream interventions are represented, keeping every node connected to the single risk. Roughly one node per 350 words meets the density guideline.  

Key limitations: The paper excerpt is short and does not provide implementation detail beyond high-level legal recommendations, so intervention nodes rely on mild inference and have low maturity scores. Quantitative evidence strength is limited, reducing edge confidence to medium.
